name: Juana Inés de la Cruz
info: Juana Inés de la Cruz (1648–1695), known as Sor Juana, was a Hieronymite nun in Mexico City and a Novohispanic poet, dramatist and philosopher of the Baroque, remembered for her verse, her plays and her defence of women's right to education.

facts.born: 12 November 1648 at San Miguel Nepantla, near Mexico City, New Spain; born outside marriage to Pedro Manuel de Asuaje y Vargas-Machuca, a Spanish navy captain from the Canary Islands, and Isabel Ramírez de Santillana, a criolla woman (two baptism registrations, of 1648 and 1651, are attributed to her and remain a matter of debate)
facts.died: 17 April 1695 in Mexico City, aged 46, after ministering to other nuns stricken during a plague; Carlos de Sigüenza y Góngora delivered the eulogy at her funeral
facts.role: Hieronymite nun in the Convent of Santa Paula (San Jerónimo), Mexico City, from 1669; earlier lady-in-waiting at the viceregal court; poet, dramatist and writer of prose treatises
facts.known: First Dream (Primero sueño); the love poetry of Inundación castálida; the comedies Los empeños de una casa and Amor es más laberinto; Hombres necios; the Carta Atenagórica (1690); the Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz (1691); her defence of women's education

t: Born outside marriage near Mexico City, Juana Inés taught herself from her grandfather's books, was tested before the viceroy's learned guests as a teenager, and in 1669 entered the Hieronymite convent so that she could study as she wished.

In the convent she wrote the philosophical poem First Dream, love poems, comedies and villancicos, and corresponded with and was supported by viceroys and vicereines who had her work published in Spain.

After the Carta Atenagórica was published without her permission in 1690 and she answered her critics in the Respuesta, she was reprimanded, and by 1693 she seemingly stopped writing; she died in 1695 after nursing her sisters in a plague.
dyk: Sor Juana is said to have learned Latin in only twenty lessons, and she reportedly cut her own hair as a punishment whenever she failed to learn something she had set herself.
ev: Born at San Miguel Nepantla, near Mexico City, on 12 November, outside marriage
At sixteen goes to live in Mexico City, where she becomes a lady-in-waiting at the court of the Viceroy, the Marquis of Mancera
Enters the Hieronymite convent, where she takes the name Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz and stays until her death
Her comedy Los empeños de una casa is first performed on 4 October, during celebrations for the birth of the Viceroy's first son
Inundación castálida, her first volume of poetry, is published in Madrid
The Bishop of Puebla publishes her critique of a sermon by António Vieira as the Carta Atenagórica, without her permission
Writes the Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz defending women's right to education, and is reprimanded and ordered to stop writing
Dies on 17 April, aged 46, after ministering to nuns stricken during a plague

sections.early:
Juana Inés de Asbaje y Ramírez de Santillana was born on 12 November 1648 at San Miguel Nepantla, near Mexico City. She was a daughter born outside marriage to Pedro Manuel de Asuaje y Vargas-Machuca, a Spanish navy captain from the Canary Islands who was involved in colonial transatlantic shipping and trade, and Isabel Ramírez de Santillana, a criolla woman whose father leased the Hacienda de Panoayan. Her father was absent from her early life, and she spent her infancy among her mother's family at that hacienda. Two baptism registrations, one of 1648 under the name Juana and one of 1651 under the name Inés, are attributed to her, and which is hers is still a matter of research and debate.

As a child she often hid in the hacienda chapel to read her grandfather's books from the adjoining library, despite the limits placed on girls' access to education. She reportedly learned to read and write by the age of three, could do accounts by five, and at eight composed a poem on the Eucharist. She began Latin under Martín de Olivas, and it is said that she learned it in only twenty lessons. Scholars long believed she learned Nahuatl as a child and wrote short poems in it, but more recent research has challenged this.

She was sent to Mexico City, a city of around 50,000 people, to live with relatives: one account of her early life dates this to 1656, to a maternal aunt and uncle, and another to 1664, when she was sixteen. She asked her mother's permission to dress as a male student to attend the university there, which was not granted, and she studied privately.
sections.rise:
Through her family's connections Juana Inés became a lady-in-waiting at the court of the Viceroy of New Spain, Antonio Sebastián de Toledo, Marquis of Mancera, where she came under the tutelage of the Vicereine, Eleonora del Carretto. When she was seventeen the Viceroy, wishing to test her learning, invited several theologians, jurists, philosophers and poets to a meeting at which she had to answer many questions unprepared and explain difficult points on scientific and literary subjects. Her answers impressed those present and helped to establish her reputation as an intellectual, and her fame spread throughout New Spain. She was much admired at court and received several proposals of marriage, which she declined.

In 1667 she entered the monastery of St Joseph, a community of Discalced Carmelite nuns, as a postulant and stayed only a few months. In 1669 she entered the monastery of the Hieronymite nuns, whose rules were more relaxed, and took the name Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, probably in reference to Sor Juana de la Cruz Vázquez Gutiérrez, a Spanish nun whose intellectual accomplishments earned her one of the few dispensations for women to preach the gospel. Another possible namesake was Saint John of the Cross. She said she chose the convent because she wanted "to have no fixed occupation which might curtail my freedom to study." Octavio Paz and Diane Marting hold that her decision came from her refusal to marry, and that the convent gave her authority and freedom without marriage.
sections.deeds:
From 1669 until her death Sor Juana remained cloistered in the Convent of Santa Paula of the Hieronymite order in Mexico City, where she studied, wrote and collected a large library. She turned her quarters into a salon visited by the female intellectual elite of New Spain, including the vicereines Eleonora del Carretto and María Luisa Gonzaga, Countess of Paredes de Nava, and she became close to the scholar Carlos de Sigüenza y Góngora. The Viceroy and Vicereine were her patrons and had her writings published in Spain. Her first volume of poems, Inundación castálida, appeared in Madrid in 1689 through the Countess of Paredes.

Her long philosophical poem First Dream describes a soul that, while the body sleeps, rises to the summit of its own intellect and tries to grasp all creation in a single act of intuition. Overwhelmed, it turns to step-by-step reasoning with Aristotle's ten categories, and that method too reaches its limit. Her comedy Los empeños de una casa was first performed on 4 October 1683 and Amor es más laberinto on 11 February 1689, and she also wrote villancicos, a loa to The Divine Narcissus and a treatise on music, El Caracol, which is now lost. She wrote the Autodefensa Espiritual to her confessor in 1682, arguing that women have the same rational souls as men and should be free to study.
sections.opponents:
In November 1690 Manuel Fernández de Santa Cruz, Bishop of Puebla, published without her permission her critique of a sermon given forty years earlier by the Portuguese Jesuit António Vieira, under the title Carta Atenagórica, himself writing as "Sor Filotea". In it she argued that Christ's greatest act of love was to preserve human free will, and many scholars read the treatise as also an implicit challenge to male intellectual authority in the Church. The Bishop added a letter of his own saying she should turn from secular studies to religious ones. He agreed with her criticisms of Vieira but held that, as a woman, she should devote herself to prayer and give up her writings.

She answered in the Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz, defending women's right to formal education and to act as intellectual authorities and teachers of other women. She wrote, quoting an Aragonese poet and echoing Teresa of Ávila, that "One can perfectly well philosophize while cooking supper." In 1691 she was reprimanded and ordered to stop writing after a private letter on women's education became public. Francisco de Aguiar y Seijas, Archbishop of Mexico, joined other high officials in condemning her "waywardness", and she was also criticised for believing that her writing could achieve the same charitable ends as community work.
sections.last:
By 1693 Sor Juana seemingly stopped writing to avoid official censure. There is no undisputed evidence that she renounced writing, but documents show her agreeing to undergo penance. Her name is affixed to one in 1694, though the tone of the supposed handwritten penitentials is rhetorical and authoritarian, unlike her usually lyrical style; one is signed "Yo, la Peor de Todas" ("I, the worst of all women"). She is said to have sold her library of more than 4,000 volumes and her musical and scientific instruments, and to have turned to charity towards the poor. Other sources report that her defiance of the Church led to the confiscation of her books and instruments, although the Bishop himself agreed with the contents of her letters.

She died on 17 April 1695, aged 46, after ministering to other nuns who had fallen ill during a plague. Sigüenza y Góngora delivered the eulogy at her funeral. Of more than one hundred unpublished works only a few of her writings survive, and according to Octavio Paz they were saved by the vicereine. Further volumes of her work were printed in Barcelona in 1693 and 1701, and a collection of her poems in Valencia in 1709.
sections.legacy:
Her contemporaries nicknamed her "The Tenth Muse", "The Mexican Phoenix" and "The Phoenix of America". Octavio Paz is credited with re-establishing her importance in modern times through his 1982 book Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz o las trampas de la fe, in which he argued that her works were the most important body of poetic work produced in the Americas until the arrival of Emily Dickinson and Walt Whitman. In the twenty-first century many Latin American philosophers and scholars read her as a feminist before the time of feminism, though scholars differ over how to read her. The Mexican writer Luis Felipe Fabre criticises Sorjuanista scholarship for making her either a heretic or a lesbian, and asks for a more complex, many-layered conversation.

She has been presented as a candidate for Catholic sainthood, a symbol of Mexican nationalism, and a figure for freedom of speech, women's rights and sexual diversity. Her name was inscribed in gold on the wall of honour of the Mexican Congress in 1995, and she appears on Mexican banknotes. The San Jerónimo convent where she lived for her last 27 years is today the University of the Cloister of Sor Juana, founded by the Mexican government in 1979. In 2022 the Episcopal Church of the United States added her feast, 18 April, to its liturgical calendar.

summary: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz (1648–1695), born near Mexico City, entered a Hieronymite convent in 1669 and wrote philosophical and love poetry, comedies and treatises. After a public quarrel with Church officials over women's education she was reprimanded, and she died in 1695 after nursing nuns stricken in a plague.
references: Octavio Paz, Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz o las trampas de la fe (Fondo de Cultura Económica, 1982)
Pamela Kirk Rappaport, Sor Juana Inés De La Cruz: Religion, Art, and Feminism (Continuum, 1998)
notes: Early life: the article says she was sent to Mexico City in 1656 (to her aunt and uncle) and again 'in 1664, at the age of 16'; both are given in the early section, attributed to 'one account' and 'another'. The event list uses 1664, when the article places the viceregal court.
Baptism: the article gives registrations of 1648 (Juana) and 1651 (Inés) as debated; birth date 12 November 1648 follows the lead, start 1648.

Books: the article says both that she was forced in 1694 to sell her library and that other sources report confiscation; both given, and the dates left as the article has them (the 'forced to sell' sentence names 1694). The 'More than 4,000 volumes' is 'said to'.
Autodefensa: the article dates it 1682, and calls it 'ten years before she severs ties' after the Respuesta (1691), which does not fit; the 1682 date only is used.
The article says both that Sor Juana 'chose to become a nun' because of study and that Paz/Marting say it was refusal of marriage; both given as attributed.

Nahuatl: the article says scholars long believed she learned it and that recent research challenges this; given as such. Her Villancico 224 in Nahuatl and 'her own indigenous identity' (Gomez, Gaspar de Alba) are left out as contested.

Left out: the Second Celestina attribution dispute, Hombres Necios details, the 1970s bones and medallion controversy, Frida Kahlo comparisons, the Primero sueño summary beyond the core, Yugar's and Powell's arguments, philanthropic organisation named CORA, and the whole Popular culture section.
Fact left out of 'died': the article's lead says she died after catching plague while treating her sisters; used as 'ministering to other nuns stricken during a plague'.

The article's 'Early life' summary has her 'condemned by the Bishop of Puebla' for criticism of misogyny and also says the Bishop agreed with her; the section on opponents follows the detailed account and does not say 'condemned'.
Lead says she wrote 'Hieronymite nun ... composer'; only the villancico Madre, la de los primores is attributed to her as music and is not mentioned.
